strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question: how to make diffusion-model visual representations task-adaptive for robotic control without fine-tuning the diffusion backbone. The motivation is clear and well connected to prior work on frozen representations, Stable Diffusion features, and prompt conditioning.

The empirical finding that naive text prompts can hurt control performance is interesting and potentially useful. The cross-attention visualizations provide a plausible explanation that text-image grounding is unreliable in simulated robotics domains.

ORCA is conceptually simple: learn task prompts and frame-dependent visual prompts under the behavior cloning objective while keeping the diffusion model frozen. This makes the method easy to understand and reasonably modular.

The paper evaluates on three common simulated robotics suites, with comparisons to CLIP, VC-1, SCR, text prompting, CoOp, and TADP. ORCA improves mean performance on DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit, and the component ablation supports that task and visual prompts are complementary.
The manuscript is generally readable, with useful figures, ablations on components/layers/timesteps, and an efficiency comparison.
weaknesses: The central attribution is not fully isolated. ORCA introduces a DINOv2 vision encoder for visual prompts, additional trainable projection layers, and learned task prompts. There is no decisive baseline using DINOv2 features alone, DINOv2 concatenated with SCR features, or a similarly parameterized trainable adapter without diffusion cross-attention. As a result, the claimed benefit of conditioning diffusion models, rather than simply adding a strong visual encoder and trainable modules, is not completely supported.

The evaluation breadth is limited to 12 simulated tasks with few demonstrations and per-task learning. There is no real-robot evaluation, no cross-task or cross-domain generalization study, and no evidence that the learned prompts transfer beyond the trained task/environment.

Several reported gains are modest relative to variance, especially on saturated MetaWorld tasks. The paper reports three seeds but does not provide significance tests or confidence intervals, and some tasks have high standard deviations, making the robustness of improvements less clear.

The protocol reports the best success rates among online evaluation trials, which can bias results upward through model selection on evaluation rollouts. The manuscript should clarify validation/model-selection procedures and whether all baselines receive identical evaluation-budget tuning.

The comparison to frozen representation baselines is somewhat uneven because ORCA has 10.6M learnable parameters and uses an additional frozen DINOv2 encoder, while VC-1/SCR are largely frozen feature extractors. The latency and parameter overhead are reported, but the performance-efficiency tradeoff is not deeply analyzed.

The mechanistic explanation based on cross-attention maps is suggestive but not conclusive. Attention visualizations do not prove causal grounding, and the paper would be stronger with perturbation/occlusion tests or prompt-token ablations that directly link attended regions to policy behavior.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. Important details such as policy architecture, optimizer settings, learning rates, demonstration collection/source, image preprocessing, exact evaluation episodes, and whether code/checkpoints will be released are not sufficiently specified in the main text.

There are some presentation and notation issues: Eq. 3 appears to mix task and visual prompt notation, the text says task prompt pv in one place, and the compression-layer pseudocode uses BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution producing compress_dim channels. These are likely fixable, but they reduce confidence in implementation clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: making diffusion-model visual representations more task-adaptive for imitation learning in robotic control without fine-tuning the full diffusion backbone.
weaknesses: The central novelty is limited. ORCA mainly combines known ideas: prompt tuning, dense visual prompts from a frozen encoder, Stable Diffusion feature extraction, and behavior-cloning training. The paper does not convincingly show a conceptually new mechanism beyond adapting existing prompt-learning machinery to robotic-control benchmarks.

The empirical support is narrower than the claims suggest. All evaluations are simulated and cover only 12 tasks across DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit, with 2-5 demonstrations and three seeds. This is not enough to support broad claims about robotic control or task-adaptive representations, especially without real-robot or stronger distribution-shift tests.

The baseline comparison is not fully convincing. ORCA adds DINOv2 visual prompts and learnable prompt/projection parameters, while key baselines such as CLIP, VC-1, and SCR are largely frozen-feature methods. The paper does not compare against similarly task-adapted/fine-tuned visual encoders, lightweight adapters on VC-1/SCR, or other parameter-matched alternatives, so the source of the gains is ambiguous.

The method may owe much of its improvement to extra trainable capacity and DINOv2 features rather than better conditioning of diffusion models. The ablations remove task and visual prompts, but do not sufficiently isolate the contribution of the diffusion backbone versus DINOv2, the compression layer, prompt capacity, or simple adapter-based alternatives under matched compute and parameter budgets.

The reported gains are mixed in magnitude and sometimes within large variance. For example, several DMC task standard deviations are substantial, and some components hurt individual tasks. The paper emphasizes mean improvements but gives limited statistical analysis or significance testing.

The efficiency story is weak. The method uses 480.1M parameters and 48ms latency versus 303.3M/11ms for VC-1 and 382.9M/26ms for SCR. This is a large cost increase for relatively modest average improvements, and the practical implications for closed-loop robotic control are under-discussed.

The causal explanation based on cross-attention maps is speculative. The paper argues that noisy text grounding explains degraded performance and that learned visual prompts capture task-relevant dynamics, but the evidence is mostly qualitative attention visualizations rather than controlled tests of grounding quality or action-relevant information.

Reproducibility has gaps. Important implementation details are still underspecified, including exact feature extraction choices, prompt initialization/training behavior, policy architecture details, evaluation protocol details such as best-checkpoint selection, and how hyperparameters were selected across tasks.

There are presentation and technical clarity issues, including notation mistakes around task/visual prompts in the objective and compression-layer pseudocode that appears inconsistent with the BatchNorm channel dimension. These are fixable, but they reinforce the sense that the manuscript is not yet polished enough for a top-tier acceptance.

Overall, the paper has a plausible idea and some encouraging simulated results, but the limited novelty, insufficiently fair baselines, high computational cost, and under-isolated source of improvement make the current evidence too weak for acceptance.

strengths: The paper asks a well-motivated and timely question: how to condition text-to-image diffusion representations for robotic control rather than using them as frozen, task-agnostic encoders. The negative result for naive text prompts is interesting and useful, especially because it contrasts with prior diffusion-perception work.

The proposed ORCA design is technically plausible and fairly simple: learn task prompts and frame-dependent visual prompts while keeping Stable Diffusion frozen, then train them end-to-end with behavior cloning. This is a clean contribution with a clear connection to the observed grounding failures of text conditions.

The empirical results are consistently positive across three standard simulated control suites. ORCA improves over SCR and text/prompting baselines on DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit, with especially meaningful gains on DMC mean score and Adroit mean success rate.

The paper includes useful ablations: task-only vs visual-only vs combined prompts, U-Net layer selection, diffusion timestep selection, latency/parameter reporting, and attention-map visualizations. These analyses support the main design choices rather than only reporting final scores.

The manuscript is generally clear and easy to follow, with a coherent motivation, method, and experimental narrative. The appendix provides concrete prompt descriptions and baseline details that improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation is entirely in simulation and covers only 12 tasks, with two Adroit tasks and five tasks each from DMC and MetaWorld. This is reasonable for a first study, but it limits the strength of claims about robotic control broadly, especially for real-world visual domain shift where diffusion priors may behave differently.

The comparison is not fully isolating the effect of the proposed conditioning. ORCA introduces DINOv2-derived visual prompts and about 10.6M learnable parameters, while the strongest task-agnostic baselines are largely frozen. A DINOv2-only representation baseline, or a baseline with comparable trainable adapter capacity, would better establish that the gains come from conditioning the diffusion model rather than from adding a strong auxiliary visual encoder and trainable projection layers.

Some reported improvements are modest relative to variance or saturation. For example, several MetaWorld tasks are already near 100% success for multiple methods, and some gains over TADP/CoOp are small. The strongest evidence is on DMC and Adroit, but even there Cheetah-run has high variance.

The evaluation protocol reports the best success rates among online evaluation trials, which may overstate performance compared with final checkpoint or fixed model selection criteria. More detail on checkpoint selection and statistical testing would make the evidence stronger.

Efficiency remains a practical concern: the proposed method is substantially heavier and slower than VC-1 and SCR according to the paper's own appendix. The 48 ms latency and 480M parameters may be acceptable in some settings, but the paper does not deeply discuss deployment constraints for real-time control.

Reproducibility is decent but incomplete. Important details such as optimizer settings, learning rates, exact policy architecture, demo generation/source, image preprocessing, evaluation episode counts, and random seed handling are not fully specified in the extracted manuscript. The pseudocode for the compression layer also appears to have a BatchNorm dimension inconsistency, and Eq. 3 has confusing prompt notation, which should be corrected.

The attention-map analysis is suggestive but not conclusive. It helps motivate the method, but the causal link between improved grounding maps and policy performance is not rigorously established. Additional quantitative grounding or representation analyses would strengthen this part.

strengths: The paper asks a clear and relevant question: how conditioning should be used when repurposing text-to-image diffusion features for robotic control, rather than assuming text prompts transfer from standard vision tasks.

The proposed ORCA design is technically plausible and simple: learned task prompts provide task-level adaptation while dense visual prompts provide frame-specific conditioning, with the diffusion backbone kept frozen.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for a robotics representation paper, covering DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit, and additional LIBERO-Long results, with comparisons to CLIP, VC-1, SCR, text-prompt baselines, CoOp, and TADP.

Ablations support the main design choices: task and visual prompts are individually useful but strongest together, early/mid U-Net layers work best, timestep choice matters, and different visual encoders for visual prompts are examined.
The paper gives useful diagnostic evidence for why naive text conditioning can fail in control, including cross-attention visualizations showing poor grounding for some simulated domains.
weaknesses: A key missing baseline is a simple fusion or concatenation of SCR/Stable-Diffusion features with DINOv2 features, or a comparable learned adapter using the same extra visual encoder. Since ORCA adds DINOv2 and 10.6M trainable parameters, the results do not fully isolate the benefit of conditioning the diffusion model versus adding a strong auxiliary representation.

The evaluation is entirely simulated and mostly uses small selected task subsets. The claims about robotic control usefulness would be stronger with real-robot evidence or a clearer justification that the selected tasks cover the relevant failure modes.

The protocol reports the best success rate among online evaluation trials for MetaWorld and Adroit, which can overstate performance compared with final checkpoint or average-over-training evaluation. This matters because several gains are modest relative to standard deviations.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as policy architecture, optimizer and learning-rate schedules, exact feature dimensions/layers, dataset/demo generation, evaluation episode counts, and code availability are not sufficiently specified in the main text. The use of Gemini 2.5 captions also introduces a proprietary dependency for some baselines.

Some technical presentation issues suggest carelessness: Eq. 3 appears to confuse task and visual prompt notation, the compression-layer pseudocode uses BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution to compress_dim, and Section 6.5 repeats the same visualization paragraph. These do not invalidate the idea but reduce confidence in implementation clarity.

The efficiency story is mixed: ORCA has substantially more total parameters and nearly doubles SCR latency according to the appendix. The paper should be more cautious about efficiency claims, especially for real-time robotic deployment.

The comparison to newer diffusion backbones is preliminary and arguably under-tuned, e.g. SVD is restricted to 3 frames despite a native 8-frame setting. These results should be framed as exploratory rather than strong evidence about architecture choice.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant question: how to condition pretrained text-to-image diffusion representations for robotic control, rather than simply using frozen task-agnostic features.

The proposed ORCA design is intuitive: learned task prompts provide task-specific conditioning, while visual prompts inject frame-dependent information. The component ablation in Table 4 supports that using both prompts is better than either alone on the reported DMC tasks.

The manuscript includes comparisons against several diffusion-conditioning variants, plus ablations on layer choice, timestep, visual encoder choice, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. This gives more evidence than a single leaderboard table.
The reported results show consistent mean improvements over the selected baselines across DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit, and supplementary LIBERO-Long experiments.
weaknesses: The central attribution is not fully convincing. ORCA adds an external DINOv2 encoder, learnable projection layers, learned prompts, and Stable Diffusion features. The paper does not include a sufficiently controlled baseline using DINOv2 features alone under the same policy/training setup, or a matched trainable adapter on SCR/VC-1 with comparable capacity and inputs. Thus it is unclear how much of the gain comes from diffusion conditioning versus adding a strong auxiliary visual encoder and trainable modules.

The evaluation is narrow for the strength of the claims. Most experiments are on a small set of simulated MuJoCo-style tasks with very few demonstrations, and the main tables often show modest improvements within or near standard deviations on individual tasks. There is no real-robot evaluation, little evidence of robustness to visual/domain shifts, and limited assessment of generalization beyond the training task distributions.

The protocol reports the best success rate among online evaluation trials for MetaWorld and Adroit, which can overstate performance relative to final or averaged evaluation checkpoints. This choice is material because many success-rate differences are small and averaged over only three seeds.

Several comparisons are not fully fair or complete. ORCA has 480M total parameters and 48ms latency versus 303M/11ms for VC-1 and 383M/26ms for SCR, yet the main SOTA framing does not sufficiently account for this cost. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning baselines are only shown on Adroit, not across the main benchmark suite.

Important implementation details are underspecified or internally inconsistent, hurting reproducibility. The policy architecture, optimization hyperparameters, data collection/demonstration details, evaluation episode counts, prompt initialization details, and exact feature extraction dimensions are not described enough to reproduce the results. The compression-layer pseudocode also appears incorrect, using BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution to compress_dim.

There are technical and notation issues that make the method harder to trust. The paper swaps or duplicates symbols for task and visual prompts in places, repeats the same visualization paragraph in Section 6.5, and contains equation/text inconsistencies around the condition C* and prompt variables.

The motivation against text prompts is plausible but not deeply established. The cross-attention visualizations are anecdotal, and the claim that text conditioning fails due to domain gap is not rigorously tested against alternative captioning/prompting strategies, task-language specifications, or robotic-domain language descriptions.

The paper’s contribution is incremental relative to existing work on diffusion features, prompt learning, and visual prompting. It combines known ingredients in a useful way, but the evidence does not yet convincingly establish a broadly reliable or clearly superior approach for robotic control.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: how to make pretrained text-to-image diffusion representations task-adaptive for vision-based robotic control without fine-tuning the full diffusion model. The observation that ordinary text prompts and caption prompts can hurt control performance is interesting and relevant beyond the specific method.

ORCA is technically coherent. The separation between learnable task prompts, which encode task-level grounding, and dense visual prompts, which vary by frame, is a sensible design for control from video observations. The method is also relatively simple to integrate into behavior cloning: the prompts and policy are trained with the standard BC objective while the diffusion model remains frozen.

The experimental evidence is fairly broad for a robotics/control representation paper. Results are reported on DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit, with additional LIBERO-Long results in the supplement. ORCA improves the mean performance over CLIP, VC-1, SCR, text-prompted diffusion baselines, CoOp, and TADP; the gains are especially clear on DMC mean performance and Adroit mean success rate.

The ablations support the main claims. The component analysis shows that task and visual prompts are both useful and work best together; the layer-selection and timestep ablations justify important implementation choices; and the appendix includes comparisons to alternative visual encoders, stronger pretrained representations, different diffusion backbones, and fine-tuning/adaptation baselines.

The qualitative cross-attention visualizations help explain why text conditions sometimes fail and how learned task/visual prompts behave differently across frames. This makes the paper more convincing than a purely metric-driven contribution.

The paper is generally clear and reproducible at the algorithmic level, with useful implementation details on benchmarks, demonstrations, baselines, prompt text, layer choices, and latency/parameter counts.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than transformative. Learnable prompts, visual prompts, prompt tuning, and diffusion features are all established ideas; the main contribution is a well-executed adaptation and empirical study for robotic control. This is valuable, but the method is more an effective composition than a fundamentally new representation-learning principle.

The evaluation is still mostly in simulated environments. DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit, and LIBERO are useful, but the paper’s claims about robotic control would be stronger with real-robot evidence or at least a more explicit analysis of sim-to-real robustness.

Some gains are modest or occur on saturated tasks. For example, MetaWorld already has several methods near 90-93% mean success and Drawer-open is saturated at 100%, so the headline state-of-the-art claim should be read with some caution. Per-task improvements are not uniformly large, and statistical significance is not analyzed beyond three-seed standard deviations.

The method has nontrivial computational overhead. The appendix reports 480.1M total parameters and 48 ms latency versus 382.9M/26 ms for SCR and 303.3M/11 ms for VC-1. This does not invalidate the contribution, but it weakens the practicality claim for real-time or resource-constrained robotic systems, especially since hardware and deployment constraints are not deeply discussed.

The comparison to modern robot foundation/VLA approaches is mostly discussed rather than experimentally tested. The authors give reasonable motivation for focusing on efficient specialist agents, but the boundary between ORCA’s applicability and large VLA-style policies remains underexplored.

The paper has a few presentation and reproducibility blemishes. Equation/notation around task and visual prompts is somewhat confusing, the visualization subsection is duplicated on page 8, and the compression-layer pseudocode appears to use BatchNorm2d with the wrong channel dimension after the convolution. These are likely fixable, but they reduce confidence in implementation exactness.

The limitations section is narrow, focusing mainly on Stable Diffusion v1.5/U-Net architecture. Other important limitations, such as real-world deployment, sensitivity to demonstration quality, prompt length choices, latency, and behavior under out-of-distribution camera views or task variants, deserve fuller treatment.
